steps.message: I read the Go test file first so the classification reflects what each test asserts, not just its name.

This is a Go package using the standard testing library. Go has no attribute-based tag mechanism the way MSTest, xUnit, or NUnit do — there is no [TestCategory] or [Trait] equivalent to insert — so this is a report-only case. I did not modify calculator_test.go; it is byte-for-byte unchanged, with no build tags, no t.Skip calls, and no comment markers injected. Here is the classification as a report.

| Test | Group | Reasoning |
|------|-------|-----------|
| TestAdd_ValidInputs_ReturnsSum | happy-path / positive | Adds 2+3 and asserts 5, a normal success case |
| TestDivide_ValidInputs_ReturnsQuotient | happy-path / positive | Divides 10/2, asserts no error and quotient 5 |
| TestDivide_ByZero_ReturnsError | error-path / negative | Divides by zero and asserts a non-nil error — the one error-path test, also a boundary (zero divisor) |
| TestAdd_ZeroOperands_ReturnsZero | happy-path / positive | Adds 0+0, a valid boundary input that still succeeds |

Distribution summary: 3 happy-path (positive) tests to 1 error-path (negative) test. TestDivide_ByZero_ReturnsError is the sole negative/error-path case; the other three verify successful behaviour, two of them (ByZero and ZeroOperands) sitting on the zero boundary.

Because Go expresses categories through naming and build tags rather than attributes, I did not invent a C#-style attribute. If you want these traits to be selectable, adopt a project-wide convention such as a `//go:build integration` build tag on integration files, a `*_negative_test.go` file-name suffix, or `testing.Short()` gating — say the word and I can apply whichever convention your team prefers. Until then this remains a report and your source is untouched.
